cognate: Arm. ołǰ 'whole, healthy' ~ Lat. saluus/salue (*solh₂-u̯o-); ełbayr ~ frater addressed in the same greeting
drift_or_renewal: Arm. copula renewed (linim ipv. ler, not *h₁es-); Lat. has both salue (denominative ipv.) and the exact adj.+copula type saluos sis; Germanic renews the adjective (wes hāl, heill ver þú, *kóh₂ilo-) in the same figure
shared_syntax: salutation: adjective 'whole' + 2sg imperative/optative of 'be', addressed to the hearer, often with vocative 'brother'
context: Movses: royal letter to Arsaces from his 'younger brother' Vałaršak, closing Ołǰ ler; elsewhere Ołǰ ler, ... sireli ełbayr (1823) and plural Ołǰ lerukʻ in Agathangelos edicts. Plautus: meeting greeting frater mi salue; saluos sis Mnesiloche. Both are fixed greeting/leave formulas between kin or peers
phrase: 'be whole!' as greeting: Arm. ołǰ ler ~ Lat. saluos sis / salue (Gk. οὖλε, recalled)
note: Health-wish greetings are cross-linguistically common and Arm. epistolary ołǰ ler also renders Gk. ἔρρωσο/χαῖρε, so the figure alone is weak; what argues for inheritance is the same root *solh₂- in the same formula type in Latin and Armenian, plus the Homeric greeting οὖλε. Irish slán (same root) only gives 'bí slán' as a healing command in saints' lives, not a greeting.

cognate: Arm. ayr ~ Skt. nara (*h₂nér-); Arm. ji ~ Skt. haya- (*ǵʰey- 'drive' derivative 'horse')
drift_or_renewal: Greek and Vedic carry the same merism with *h₁éḱwos (ἵπποι/aśva-); Armenian (where *h₁éḱwos survives only as ēš 'ass') and epic Sanskrit use the *ǵʰey- word
shared_syntax: coordinated pair 'man and horse' (Arm. collective singular, Skt. plural instr./acc.) standing for an army's whole force
context: Agathangelos: demons appear like a host of 'man and horse', cavalry and infantry; also 'great multitude of man and horse', 'leader of man and horse'. MBh: battlefield strewn with fallen horses and men; Il. 10.338 throng of horses and men
phrase: 'men and horses' = army: Arm. ayr ew ji ~ Skt. hayāḥ narāḥ ca (Gk. ἵπποι τε καὶ ἄνδρες, Ved. nṛ́bhir áśvaiḥ)
note: The merism is natural military language and the horse word differs inside the attested set; the cognate match rests on Armenian and epic Sanskrit both using the *ǵʰey- noun, which may be separate innovations. Claimed only as a low-confidence carrier of a widespread *h₂nér-/horse merism.
